Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I distract myself with something else
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette:
David is a 63-year-old rabbi who came to treatment after years of trying to contain a life organized around narrow pockets of safety. He was born in the United States, but the trauma he returns to began when he was a boy in a family that had fled violence and displacement. In the sessions he does not speak about it in broad historical terms first; he speaks in moments. He remembers being crowded with family members in temporary housing after they had escaped, remembers adults speaking in urgent voices he could not fully follow, and most of all remembers armed men during the flight and its aftermath—how quickly an ordinary object could become a weapon in someone’s hand, how shouting could turn a room electric, how a hand on his shoulder without warning did not feel like comfort but like capture. In his memory, the danger is not abstract. It is the sight of something raised to strike, the crack of a voice, the shock of being grabbed before he understood what was happening.

He describes those memories as old and far away, but his body does not behave as if they are over. If someone touches him unexpectedly, even lightly, he jolts hard before he can think. When he sees a weapon, or even an object that could be used as one, his attention narrows immediately. Loud shouting, even when it is only an argument overheard in public, makes him feel as though the room has changed shape around him. What unsettles him most is not only the reaction itself but the meaning he has given it over the years. He has come to believe that his own body is an enemy of sorts, launching him into alarm when he is standing in a sanctuary, a grocery store, or his own home. He says with shame that he cannot rely on himself; if his body can betray him so quickly, then he does not trust his own steadiness. He also carries a harsh comparison with an imagined stronger person. Somebody else, he is certain, would have done something, would have stopped what happened, would not have remained frightened in the way he did.

Over the years, these convictions settled into the structure of his days. At synagogue he is attentive to where he sits and stands, though he tries not to draw attention to it. In meetings, at communal meals, even during services, he chooses places that let him see the door and avoid being hemmed in. He notices where people’s hands are, who is moving behind him, which voices are rising. Congregants know him as thoughtful and pastoral, but they do not see how much effort goes into tracking the room when concentration slips away from the prayer book or the person speaking across from him. During pastoral visits or committee meetings, he sometimes realizes he has lost the thread of conversation because part of him has been occupied with who entered the room, whether someone came too close behind his chair, or whether an object on a desk caught his eye in the wrong way.

His world has gradually narrowed around a small number of places where he feels he can truly exhale. Home is one of them, and his office at the synagogue can be another when the door is positioned the way he wants it and interruptions are limited. Outside those spaces he is tense and vigilant. He manages by redirecting himself whenever memories or sensations surge—burying himself in administrative tasks, sermon preparation, reading, anything that can pull his mind sideways. He knows this as distraction, though he experiences it simply as getting through the day.

The cost has been most visible in his relationship. He is partnered, but emotional closeness has become difficult terrain. He avoids intimacy not because he does not care, but because closeness leaves him feeling exposed and unguarded. Unprepared touch is especially hard; even affectionate contact can produce a recoil he cannot hide quickly enough. He then turns his anger inward. Rather than blaming the past, he tells himself he deserves to suffer because of what happened, as if ongoing distress were a fitting sentence for not having been the kind of person who could have prevented it.

He sought help now after several incidents in quick succession left him frightened by how small his safe world had become. A raised voice during a heated exchange at the synagogue, a congregant touching his arm from behind to get his attention, and the sight of a security officer’s weapon at a community event each stayed with him long after the moment passed. He found himself unable to focus on sermon writing and increasingly reluctant to attend events he once would have led with ease. What finally brought him in was not only the exhaustion of living this way, but the fear that he would continue retreating from his partner, his congregation, and his calling. He says he hopes for “some peace with my own body,” and what he fears most is that safety will always mean making his life smaller.
